title: Musculoskeletal system: bones, joints and muscles
note: Core roots: oste/o bone, arthr/o joint, chondr/o cartilage, my/o muscle, ten/o or tendin/o tendon. Watch myel/o: it means bone marrow or spinal cord, not muscle. Many bones have their own roots, such as crani/o, cost/o, stern/o and vertebr/o.

read.title: Builders and breakers
text: Bone is living tissue that is constantly rebuilt. Two kinds of cell share the work, and their names show how word parts carry meaning. An osteoblast is a bone-forming cell: oste/o means bone and -blast means a formative or immature cell. An osteoclast breaks bone down, from -clast, meaning to break. Their balance keeps the skeleton strong; when breakdown outpaces building, bone becomes porous, which is the literal meaning of osteoporosis.

Joints have their own vocabulary. Arthr/o means joint, chondr/o means cartilage, and burs/o names the small fluid-filled sacs that cushion movement. Combine them with procedure suffixes: arthroscopy views the inside of a joint, arthrocentesis draws out fluid with a needle, arthroplasty repairs or replaces the joint, and arthrodesis fuses it so it no longer moves.

Muscle terms rely on my/o. Myalgia is muscle pain and electromyography records the electrical activity of muscle. Be careful with myel/o, which looks similar but refers to bone marrow or the spinal cord. Tendons attach muscle to bone, while ligaments attach bone to bone.
